chapter_theme: Paripadal 17 and 18, to Murugan of Parankunram: worship on the hill where every festival sound meets a rival sound of nature, the crowded road from Koodal, the hill rivalling the god's other hill, lovers' sulks mended and a bard's lies refuted on it, and prayers to dwell at the god's feet with kin.

paripadal:17:1-21.reading: Carrying honeyed flowers, tender leaves, flowered cloth, cast bells and the raised leaf-spear, mixing sandal, the velan ties a ram at the guarded tree and the worshippers praise with words and with tuned song; on this hill whose trees are wet with the honey of open flowers, torch, song, fragrance, smoke and banners rise together, and those who join the god's feet evening after evening want no dwelling of the gods above; on one side the bards' lute sounds and on another the bees hum, here the flute and there the tumbi drones its tune, here the drum and there the waterfall brims, here the singing women sway and there the flower creepers sway in the north wind, here the paadini's paalai voice shows the rising and falling notes and there the peacock calls, so that, as if in rivalry, each answers the other: such is the hill of him who slew the foe.
paripadal:17:1-21.nuance: The passage is built as ten alternating sides (ஒருதிறம்), and each human performance is matched by a thing of the hill doing the same act: lute and bee, flute and tumbi, drum and falls, swaying singers and swaying creepers, the paadini's voice and the peacock's. The closing line names the god by the same word as the contest, மாறு: the slayer of the foe (மாறு அட்டான்) owns a hill where every sound meets its rival (மாறு எதிர் கோடல்). Line 8 sets the worship above heaven itself: who would want the gods' abode?

thinai_evidence.note: worship and praise of the god's hill: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து under paadaan

comparisons.vehicle: மாறுமாறு உற்றன் போல் மாறு எதிர் கோடல்
comparisons.tenor: the festival's music and the hill's own sounds answering one another side by side

paripadal:17:22-39.reading: On the road between Koodal, rich in song and fame, and Parankunram, people revel smeared with fragrant sandal, so crowded that what is near and near again is far and far, and petals loosened from the women's garlands and the men's tufts leave no room to walk; on the hill that sends its fragrance to every quarter by blameless truth and sacrifice, the smoke of agil that consumes the offerings rises here and there till the gods above blink and the unwaning sun cannot be seen; and women with bangled forearms and soft shoulders, men with garlanded chests, all leap together on the swings, so that the bees that suck the pollen of the pool flowers cannot get to them: such is the beauty of Parankunram.
paripadal:17:22-39.nuance: Each image measures the crowd by what it blocks: the near road becomes far, the fallen petals close the path, the smoke shuts out the sun and makes even the unblinking gods blink (இமைபு), and the swingers keep the bees from the pool flowers. The festival is praised by its excess, not by any rite described in detail.

thinai_evidence.note: the festival beauty of the god's hill described as praise: paadaan

paripadal:17:40-53.reading: The long white falls spread over the fields of those below without ceasing, and as those above move about, the gems they drop churn the blue paddy plots; the god's festival and the fine feasting of guests pass, hand to hand in turn, between this hill of white falls, the Vaiyai of unfailing wealth and the Koodal of the king of the maned-horse banner chariot, and that alternation is good; so the poet turns to the god, lord who rode Pinimukam, with the peacock raised on his bird banner, and says: leaving other service and praising your fame, we sing your tall hill and bow, we and our kin, that we may have days of safety.
paripadal:17:40-53.nuance: The hill, the river and the city are joined by one exchange: the falls water the fields below, and the god's festival and the feasting of guests move between the three places. பிணிமுகம் is the name of the god's mount; whether it is the elephant or the peacock is not settled from this line, which also names the peacock on the banner.

thinai_evidence.note: description of the hill's bounty ending in the closing prayer of the hymn: paadaan

paripadal:18:1-6.reading: O spear-bearer who, like the full-bellied cloud that meets the rainy season, met those who came against you in battle and broke the pride of their strength, and who in the water-spread expanse that holds up the earth destroyed the mango of Sur and his ring of attendants: this hill takes up the challenge of standing level with the hill that bears your glory.
paripadal:18:1-6.nuance: The hill is not said to equal the god's other hill outright: ஏறுமாறு ஏற்கும் makes it a contender that accepts the contest, the same language of rivalry the companion song 17 uses for the hill's sounds.

thinai_evidence.note: the god's victory over Sur sung as praise: paadaan

comparisons.vehicle: கார் எதிர்ந்து ஏற்ற கமஞ் சூல் எழிலிபோல்
comparisons.tenor: the god meeting his foes in battle

paripadal:18:7-15.reading: Seeing her man gaze at a bright peacock with gem-like eyespots and brood within, the woman of the lovely brow says she knows what he was thinking and bids him tell it and not mock her or hide it; he answers: my love, I was thinking how the peacock had stolen your bearing, and when I looked at a quail dazed in its revelry you looked at me as at a stranger; so he talks her out of the sulk, and that, says the poet, is the way of the god's hill.
paripadal:18:7-15.nuance: The quarrel turns on a look: she reads his silent gaze as thought of another woman, he turns the same gaze into praise of her, because what he was looking at had taken her nature (நின் இயல் களவு). The scene is offered as the hill's character (குன்ற இயல்பு), so the god's hill is praised by the quick mending of lovers' quarrels on it. Why the quail enters his answer is not clear.

thinai_evidence.note: a sulk at the husband's gaze, talked away: marutham's uri set on the kurinji hill

comparisons.vehicle: ஒள் ஒளி மணிப் பொறி ஆல் மஞ்ஞை
comparisons.tenor: the woman's bearing, which the peacock has stolen

paripadal:18:16-22.reading: On the lovely hill where every kind of richness blooms, she says to the bard: do you not see the marks that the hands of women with rain-cool eyes like collyrium-dark flowers have made bloom on him? we have caught the embrace that bloomed thick, and the desirable gold ornaments that bloomed on his body; bard, your song on tuned strings has bloomed only a richness of lies.
paripadal:18:16-22.nuance: Every line turns on the same phrase, வளம் பூத்த, so the hill's blooming richness, the marks on the man, the embrace and the ornaments all bloom alike, and the bard's song blooms too, but with lies. The speaker is not named; the wife is the likeliest reading of யாம் கைப்படுத்தேம், though the friend speaking for her is possible.

thinai_evidence.note: the bard's message refused because the marks of other women are seen: the marutham sulk

paripadal:18:23-30.reading: O Vel of the white-flaming spear, sun of the swift peacock and the spear: on your hill, which with its victorious peaks where the rain clouds thundered over gathered tender shoots, and with its creeper lightning that dazzles the eyes, flares, presses on and splits the dark, looks like your elephant with its bright forehead plate, stands the city where the lovely painted hall is the seat of the work of Kama's arrows.
paripadal:18:23-30.nuance: The hill is first likened to the god's own war elephant, the lightning playing the part of its gleaming forehead plate, and then holds a painted hall given over to the god of love's arrows: the war god's hill houses the love god's work.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god and his hill: paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the god's hill with its lightning

paripadal:18:31-42.reading: With groves on the dread-haunted slopes thick as a quiver full of sharp arrows, the pools brim with rain water and the clustered flowers brim with beauty; the close-packed kanthal that heralds the rains is like the hands of men defeated in war and bound, and the tumbi bees loosening the bound buds are like hands loosening the twisted strings of a lute; the wind of the dewy season has drawn on the lovely clouds the rainbow of the thunderbolt-bearer, and on the mountain, you who are skilled at the game of dice, the trees have spread soft flowers like arrows rained from a bow.
paripadal:18:31-42.nuance: Two linked images use one bud: the closed kanthal is a bound captive's hands, and the bee that opens it is a player's hand loosening lute strings, so the flower passes from an image of war to one of music. The address வல்லுப் போர் வல்லாய், to one skilled in dice, begins the dice imagery of the next lines; who is addressed is not clear.

thinai_evidence.note: description of the god's hill in the rains, within praise: paadaan

comparisons.vehicle: கட்டு யாழின் புரி நெகிழ்ப்பார் போன்றன கை
comparisons.tenor: the tumbi bees opening the bound buds
the soft flowers the trees spread

paripadal:18:43-57.reading: You skilled at rolling dice: on the mountain, with the swelling clatter of the long throw, like the din of battle, the clouds roar and stand; as the falls roar the peaks wear pearls, as the sparrows chirp the millet bends its ears, the kites gather, and the pools, with many flowers where striped bees hum, curve like the lovely rainbow set in the sky; and where strings and song join, where the sruti, flowers and lamps come together and burning agil and sandal give their fragrance, lord of the army with the war spear, may we stay at your feet without parting, with our kin, as one comes to dwell in the town that is rightly one's own.
paripadal:18:43-57.nuance: The closing prayer asks not for gifts but for dwelling: to stay at the god's feet as in one's own rightful town, never parting (பிரியாது), the same word akam uses for lovers. The run of lines 46 to 51 pairs each sound of the hill with what it brings about (falls and pearls, sparrows and millet); எருவை may be the kite or a kind of reed, and lines 43 to 46 are hard to construe.

thinai_evidence.note: the closing prayer of the hymn: paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the clatter of the dice and the clouds' roar
the pools arched with many-coloured flowers

links.note: Paripadal 8.17-28 has the hill answer back and forth (மாறுமாறு அதிர்ப்ப) with the cloud, the cock, the elephants and the caves, and the bees hum like the lute; Paripadal 17.9-21 sets the bards' lute, flute, drum, dancers and singer side by side with bees, tumbi, falls, creepers and peacock, each answering the other (மாறு எதிர் கோடல்).
links.teaches: In song 8 the echo contest is among the hill's own things and the lute only a likeness for the bees, while song 17 puts the festival's real musicians into the contest against the hill, so together they show the Parankunram echo becoming a set piece in which worshippers and mountain compete as equals.

links.note: Paripadal 9.70-85 says that on the god's hill dancers outdo dancers and bards outdo those practised in song, the skilled the skilled; Paripadal 17.9-21 matches each human performer not with another performer but with a thing of the hill doing the same act.
links.teaches: Song 9 makes the festival a rivalry of like with like among people, and song 17 widens the rival to the bee, the falls and the peacock, so the pair shows that for these poets the god's hill was praised by contest itself, and the strongest praise was to have nature enter the contest.

links.note: Thirumurugatruppadai 67-77 marks the god's dwelling on the hill west of Koodal by the bees that sleep in the lotus and hum round the pool flowers opening like eyes; Paripadal 17.37-38 says that when the swingers leap together on festival day the bees that suck the pool flowers' pollen cannot reach them.
links.teaches: The guide poem gives the hill west of Koodal at rest, its pool bees the sign of the god's ordinary dwelling, and the hymn uses the same pool bees to measure the festival, when the crowd drives them off, so the pair shows the same place on its common day and on its feast day.

links.note: Kural 43 makes the chief duty of the householder the care of ancestors, gods, guests, kin and self; Paripadal 17.42-46 says the god's festival and the fine feasting of guests pass in turn between the hill, the Vaiyai and Koodal, and the song closes with a prayer made with kin (யாமும் எம் சுற்றமும்).
links.teaches: The Kural lays the duties to god, guest and kin on one household, while the hymn shows the same duties carried by a whole region in turn, hill, river and city, so the pair shows the couplet's private order also lived as the civic round of Madurai's festivals.

links.note: Paripadal 8.10-11 says that because of the god Parankunram equals the Himalaya (பரங்குன்று இமயக் குன்றம் நிகர்க்கும்); Paripadal 18.5-6 says this hill takes up the contest to stand level with the hill that bears the god's glory (ஏறுமாறு ஏற்கும் இக் குன்று).
links.teaches: Song 8 states the equality as a settled fact granted by the god's presence, and song 18 turns it into a challenge the hill still accepts, so read together they show the Paripadal poets making Parankunram's rank against the northern mountain a standing claim each hymn renews.

links.note: Kural 1320 has the man say that even when he looks at her thinking, she flares up: whom were you thinking of as you looked? In Paripadal 18.8-14 the woman sees him gaze at a peacock and think, says she knows his thought and demands it, and he answers that he was thinking how the peacock had stolen her bearing.
links.teaches: The couplet ends on the woman's suspicion with no reply, while the hymn supplies the reply that disarms it, that the thought was of her through the bird that took her grace, so the pair shows the silent gaze as a fixed cause of sulking and the lover's answer as part of the same convention.

links.note: Kalittokai 95 has the husband say he only watched a quail fight (குறும்பூழ் போர்), and the wife turns each kind of quail fight into a figure for his affairs; in Paripadal 18.12-14 the man says he looked at the peacock and at a quail dazed with revelry, and the woman looked at him as a stranger.
links.teaches: In the Kalittokai the man's watching of birds is an alibi that the wife exposes, while in the Paripadal his gaze at birds is a lover's thought of her that he can explain away, so the pair shows the same excuse of bird-watching used once for a lie caught and once for a sulk mended on the god's hill.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 47 has the woman tell the man that her companions know he tells many lies, just like his bard; Paripadal 18.16-22 shows her making the bard see the nail marks, the embrace and the ornaments on the man and calling his song a bloom of lies (பொய் வளம் பூத்தன).
links.teaches: The Ainkurunuru gives the charge that the bard lies as his master does, and the hymn gives the proof shown to the bard's face, the marks the hill's women left, so together they show the god's festival hill as one of the places where marutham's straying was caught, with the bard's song refuted by the body.

links.note: Kuruntokai 1 says the hill of the Red One, who killed the demons till the field ran red, is thick with kanthal clusters the colour of blood (குருதிப் பூவின் குலைக்காந் தட்டே); Paripadal 18.35-36 says the close-packed kanthal of the god's hill are like the hands of men defeated in war and bound.
links.teaches: Both poets make the kanthal of Murugan's hill a sign of his war, but the Kuruntokai reads it by colour, the blood of the slain, and the Paripadal by shape, the clasped hands of the captured, so the pair shows the flower fixed as the god's war emblem while each poet chose a different basis for it.

new_concepts.gloss: the festival of the god at his shrine, with its crowds, music, offerings and feasting
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's words (Paripadal 17, line 42: தெய்வ விழவும்)

source_issues: Paripadal 17 and 18: the colophons have no thinai or thurai; only the subject செவ்வேள், the poets, the music and the pans நோதிறம் and காந்தாரம் (musical modes, not thinais) are given.

Paripadal 17 line 4: பரவினர் உரையொடு had its vowel sign ொ restored by rule (flag); not confirmed by sangamtamil.com. A line before line 9 was dropped as a modern heading (flag); the run of ஒருதிறம் clauses reads as complete.

Paripadal 18 line 7, தலைமகன் ஊடல் உணர்ப்பிக்கும் திறம், reads as a prose heading, not verse; it would account for the text having 57 lines where the source numbers its last line 56. It is kept in the unit so the line numbers stay those `show` prints.
Paripadal 18 line 10 was repaired from sangamtamil.com, and the printed line number 10 stands on line 11 (flags); a line before line 16 was dropped as a modern heading (flag).

Paripadal 18 line 18: வடு வொடு is printed as two words; read as வடுவொடு. Line 27: விரை மயில் வேல் ஞாயிறு and lines 31-32 and 42-46 (the quiver image and the address to one skilled at dice) are hard to construe.
Paripadal 17 line 46: கை ஊழ் தடுமாற்றம் is obscure; read here as the festival and feasting passing in turn between hill, river and city.
